questions.questionText: How does DBSCAN fundamentally differ from k-means in how it forms clusters?
options: DBSCAN also uses centroids, just computed differently
DBSCAN groups points by local density and connectivity, rather than distance to a single center point
questions.correctAnswer: DBSCAN groups points by local density and connectivity, rather than distance to a single center point
questions.explanation: DBSCAN chains together densely-packed core points, letting it trace clusters of arbitrary shape that a centroid-based method like k-means can't represent.

questions.questionText: What happens to points in low-density regions in DBSCAN?
options: They're forced into the nearest cluster anyway
They're labeled as noise (-1) and not assigned to any cluster
They automatically form their own single-point clusters that count toward n_clusters
DBSCAN cannot handle this case and errors out
questions.correctAnswer: They're labeled as noise (-1) and not assigned to any cluster
questions.explanation: Points that aren't within eps of enough neighbors to be core or border points are explicitly marked as noise — a built-in way to detect outliers.

questions.questionText: Unlike k-means, DBSCAN does not require you to specify:
questions.explanation: DBSCAN discovers the number of clusters automatically from the density structure of the data — you tune eps and min_samples instead of k.
